passages.happening:
“While Israel was staying in Shittim, the men began to indulge in sexual immorality with the daughters of Moab, who also invited them to the sacrifices for their gods. And the people ate and bowed down to these gods” (verses 1-2).

“So Israel joined in worshiping Baal of Peor, and the anger of the LORD burned against them” (verse 3).

God tells Moses that the leaders of the people are to be executed publicly, ‘so that His fierce anger may turn away from Israel’ (verse 4). Moses tells the judges of Israel that each must put to death those of his men who have joined in the worship of Baal of Peor (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The contrast with the last three chapters is sharp, and it is meant to be. On the heights Balaam has just said that no spell can touch Israel and that God plans no disaster for Jacob. Down on the plain, at the same time, Israel is doing to itself what no curse could do.

Shittim was Israel's last camp before the Jordan. Joshua would later send his spies from there. The promised land is in sight across the river. The last great failure of the wilderness happens on its doorstep.

The order of events in verses 1 to 3 matters. It begins with the men of Israel. The text says ‘the men began’. Then comes an invitation to a feast. In the ancient world a religious feast meant eating the meat of sacrifices in the presence of the god, so to eat was to share in that god's worship. Then comes bowing down. The Hebrew verb in verse 3 means to be yoked, like two animals in one harness. Israel, which was bound to the LORD by covenant, harnessed itself to another god.

Some scholars think the sexual acts were part of fertility rites in the worship of Baal. Others think the text describes ordinary relationships and marriages that drew the men into their partners' religion. Either way the sin joined sexual unfaithfulness to the worship of other gods. Israel's prophets later treated those as two sides of one betrayal.

Baal means lord or master. It was the title of the Canaanite god of storm and fertility, worshiped in many local forms. Baal of Peor was the god of that height, the same Peor from which Balaam had looked down.

It needs saying what the chapter is not about. It is not a judgment on the women of Moab or Midian as a people, and it is not a rule against marrying a foreigner. Moses' own wife was a Midianite. Ruth, the great-grandmother of King David, was a woman of Moab. The fault the chapter names is Israel's own: its men chose another god.

The command of verses 4 and 5 is severe. The leaders are held responsible first. The story presents it as a court acting under God's direct order to stop a judgment already falling on the whole camp. A plague is under way (verse 9).
passages.later:
Moses pointed back to this day when he spoke to the generation that survived it: “Your eyes have seen what the LORD did at Baal-peor” (Deuteronomy 4:3). “But you who held fast to the LORD your God are alive to this day, every one of you” (Deuteronomy 4:4).

Paul names it among his warnings to the church at Corinth: “We should not commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and in one day twenty-three thousand of them died” (1 Corinthians 10:8). He is writing to Christians who thought they were safe.
passages.asks: No enemy brought Israel down at Peor. Israel walked there. Ask where the real danger to your faith lies: in what others might do to you, or in what you are drawn to. And ask what feast you have been invited to that would bind you to something other than God.

passages.happening:
While Moses and the whole congregation are weeping at the entrance to the tent, an Israelite man brings a Midianite woman to his family ‘in the sight of Moses and the whole congregation’ (verse 6).

Phinehas, the son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, gets up, takes a spear, follows the man into his tent, and drives the spear through both of them. “So the plague against the Israelites was halted, but those who died in the plague numbered 24,000” (verses 8-9).

God says to Moses, “Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned My wrath away from the Israelites; for he was zealous for My sake among them” (verse 11). “Declare, therefore, that I am granting him My covenant of peace. It will be a covenant of permanent priesthood for him and his descendants” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
This is a violent scene, and it is told in two verses without comment. Then the text praises the man who did it. A reader is right to stop over that.

Several things in the story should be seen before any judgment is made.

A plague is killing thousands. The people are gathered at the sanctuary, weeping. God has already ordered the judges to carry out sentence on those who joined in the worship of Baal (verses 4-5). Into that scene a man walks with his partner in full view of everyone and goes into his tent. The man is no ordinary Israelite. He is named later as a leader of a family in the tribe of Simeon, and the woman as the daughter of a Midianite chief. It was a public act by leading people, done in front of the mourners.

Phinehas is a priest. Guarding the sanctuary and the camp's holiness was the priests' duty. The story presents him as carrying out a judgment already given, at a moment when the whole people was dying.

The word translated ‘zealous’ comes four times in verses 11 and 13. The Hebrew is the word for jealousy. God says that Phinehas acted with God's own jealousy. In the Bible God's jealousy is the love of a husband who will not share his wife with a rival. It is used of his bond with Israel.

The reward is a ‘covenant of peace’. Peace follows the violence, and that is its purpose in the story. The plague ends. The breach between God and his people is closed. Later books trace Israel's high priests through the line of Phinehas (1 Chronicles 6:4-15).

The number of the dead, 24,000, makes this the deadliest judgment in the book. The next chapter counts those who remain, and finds that the generation which left Egypt is gone.
passages.later:
A psalm remembers the day: “But Phinehas stood and intervened, and the plague was restrained. It was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations to come” (Psalm 106:30-31).

The prophets later promised a covenant of peace for the whole people: “I will make with them a covenant of peace” (Ezekiel 34:25).

The New Testament speaks of God's wrath turned away, and in a very different manner. Paul writes of Christ, “For He Himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), who reconciled people to God ‘through the cross’ (Ephesians 2:16). Phinehas turned wrath away by striking the guilty. The New Testament says that Christ turned it away by bearing it himself.
passages.hard:
Does the praise of Phinehas approve of killing in God's name? Could anyone today act as he did?

No one today may act as he did. That must be said first and plainly.

The story itself sets limits around what happened. It took place in Israel's camp, where God's tent stood, under the covenant of Sinai. A plague was killing the people. God had given a direct order of judgment through Moses. Phinehas was a priest of that sanctuary. Readers have generally taken the event as one of a kind, a judgment at a single moment in Israel's beginning, and not as leave for anyone to take a life for God's honor.

It was misused all the same. In the Maccabean revolt of the second century BC the priest Mattathias was compared to Phinehas for his zeal (1 Maccabees 2:26). In the first century AD some who took up arms against Rome claimed the same model. Christians in later ages reached for the Old Testament's wars to bless violence against people they judged to be God's enemies, as the site's guide to the violence of the Old Testament records. That was a misuse of Scripture, and it was wrong.

The New Testament points another way. Paul had been a man of exactly this kind of zeal. He describes his former life with the words ‘as to zeal, persecuting the church’ (Philippians 3:6). After he met Christ he poured the same energy into preaching and into suffering for others. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village that would not receive Jesus, “Jesus turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55). And when Peter drew a sword to defend him, Jesus told him to put it away (Matthew 26:52).

So zeal for God never gives a Christian a warrant to harm anyone: not a person of another faith, not a person who has left the faith, not a family member thought to have brought shame. No one may use this chapter to justify violence against any person or people.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

One smaller question remains. Numbers says 24,000 died. Paul says 23,000 fell ‘in one day’ (1 Corinthians 10:8). Some think Paul counts one day and Numbers the whole plague. Others think he gives a round number from memory. His point does not rest on the figure.
passages.asks: Paul kept his zeal and changed what he did with it. Ask where your own strong feeling for what is right has turned into harshness toward a person. And ask what it would look like to spend that same energy in bearing a cost for someone, as Christ did.

passages.t: The names, and a word about Midian
passages.happening:
Only now are the two named. “The name of the Israelite who was slain with the Midianite woman was Zimri son of Salu, the leader of a Simeonite family. And the name of the slain Midianite woman was Cozbi, the daughter of Zur, a tribal chief of a Midianite family” (verses 14-15).

Then God says to Moses, ‘Attack the Midianites and strike them dead’, because they acted deceitfully against Israel ‘in the matter of Peor’ (verses 17-18).
passages.hearers:
The narrator held back the names until the event was over. Given here, they explain why the act in verse 6 was so grave. Zimri was a leader. Cozbi was a chief's daughter. What they did was a public statement by people whom others followed.

The command against Midian points ahead to chapter 31, where it is carried out, and where it is revealed that the events at Peor were planned on the advice of Balaam (31:16). What he could not do with a curse he tried to do by another road. On that telling, Peor was a deliberate plan by certain leaders to break Israel from within.

Who the Midianites were needs care. They were a loose group of desert peoples who ranged widely. Moses had lived among Midianites for many years. His wife was one of them, and so was his father-in-law Jethro, who had given him wise advice. The group in view here is the one settled near Moab and allied with it against Israel. The command is not a verdict on a whole people for all time, and nothing in it gives a reason to despise any nation.

The note on chapter 31 faces the war itself, which is one of the hardest passages in the Bible.
passages.later:
The risen Jesus warns a church about the same snare: some there ‘hold to the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites so they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality’ (Revelation 2:14).

Exodus remembers a Midianite with honor. When Jethro, the priest of Midian, heard what God had done for Israel, he said, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods” (Exodus 18:11).
passages.asks: Zimri and Cozbi were leaders, and what they did in public gave others leave to do the same. Ask who watches what you do and takes it as permission. And ask whether you judge a whole people by the wrong some of them have done.
